rich_summary: Takshaka plots to kill King Parikshit despite the king’s precautions. Using deception, he sends snakes disguised as ascetics bearing offerings of fruit, kusa grass, and water. The king accepts the gifts and shares the fruit with his ministers. Inside one fruit hides Takshaka, appearing first as a tiny, ugly insect. Aware of the prophecy that he will die from the serpent’s bite, Parikshit ironically invites the creature to become Takshaka and fulfill the curse. The insect transforms, coils around the king’s neck, and fatally bites him; the palace soon burns with the serpent’s poison. After the king’s death, the people crown his young son Janamejaya, who later marries Vapushtama. The chapter then shifts to the ascetic Jaratkaru, who discovers his ancestors hanging over a pit, symbolizing a lineage on the verge of extinction and setting up a crucial future quest.

highlight_spans.why: Takshaka’s initial reflection about deceiving the king establishes the theme of illusion and cunning.
The eerie moment when the strange insect emerges from the fruit, foreshadowing the king’s doom.
Parikshit’s fatal decision to place the insect on his neck fulfills the curse and triggers the climax.
Takshaka reveals himself, coils around the king, and delivers the deadly bite.
The haunting image of Jaratkaru’s ancestors hanging by a fragile root introduces the theme of lineage and duty.

top_scenes.scene_text: A royal court at sunset where King Parikshit examines a fruit as a strange copper‑colored insect crawls out while ministers watch uneasily.
The tiny insect suddenly transforming into the great serpent Takshaka, coiling around the king’s neck as he sits on his throne.
The ascetic Jaratkaru discovering ghostly ancestors hanging upside down over a dark pit by a single fraying root while a rat gnaws at it.
